1:
The chapter turns from the instability of happiness to the misery the world is full of, and the first verse is a catalogue of who suffers. John Gill lists the oppressed by class, subjects by their prince, the stranger and the widow and the fatherless by unjust judges, the poor by the rich, servants and labourers by their masters, and reports one rabbi’s paraphrase that the writer saw these by a spirit of prophecy, foreseeing all the oppressions that would be done. He also records another rabbi’s view that the writer here calls back his earlier word about rejoicing in one’s works, though Gill notes he afterwards repeats it. Matthew Henry makes the same catalogue from the other end, servants and labourers oppressed by masters who take advantage of their necessity to impose what terms they please, debtors by cruel creditors and creditors by fraudulent debtors, tenants by hard landlords, orphans by treacherous guardians, and worst of all subjects by arbitrary princes and unjust judges; he adds the comfort that such things are done under the sun, while above the sun righteousness reigns for ever, and observes that the world is a place of weepers. Adam Clarke gives the word its full extent, any injury a man can receive in his person, his property or his good fame, and draws the plain conclusion that where the power is on the side of the oppressors there is neither protection nor comfort for the oppressed. John Wesley says the oppression may be by princes or magistrates or other potent persons, and that none afforded pity or succour.

Charles Ellicott asks the sharpest question in the chapter. Granting the traditional authorship, he wants to know what the king was about, and whether he could do nothing but express helpless despair. He does not answer it, and no other voice raises it.

The praise of the dead and the preference for the unborn are handled carefully by those who feel their weight. Wesley states the terms plainly: he judged them less miserable, and setting aside the future life, which he says the writer does not meddle with in this debate, and considering the vanity and manifold calamities of the present one, a wise man would not account it worth his while to live. Gill limits the saying in the same direction, that the judgment is made according to sense and regards the dead purely as dead, without respect to their future state, since otherwise an unborn person is not happier than those who die in Christ; and he takes the dead who are praised to be the righteous dead, taken away from the evil to come and free from their enemies. He notes that the line stands opposed to the maxim of some philosophers that a miserable being is better than none at all, and that Jewish interpreters have used it to prove the pre-existence of souls. Clarke keeps to the figure of a journey, counting those happy who have escaped from the pilgrimage of life to the place where the wicked cease from troubling and the weary are at rest, and at the next verse says only that it is better never to have been born than to have seen and suffered so many miseries. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the grammar, showing how the infinitive that opens the second verse continues the finite verb before it in an adverbially subordinate way, and they take a moment to remark that one Greek translator, by his choice of a word here and earlier, betrays himself as a Jew. Ellicott contributes one philological note, that the word rendered yet in this verse belongs to later Hebrew and occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament.
4:
Envy of honest success is the next vanity, and Matthew Henry takes it hardest. The man in view got his estate neither easily nor dishonestly but by fair dealing, and for this he is envied, the more for the reputation his honesty won him. Henry draws two lessons: what little conscience most men have, who grudge a neighbour for being more industrious and more blessed, which he calls downright diabolism, illustrating it from three pairs of rivals in the old histories; and what little comfort useful men may expect, since those who excel in virtue will always be an eye-sore to those who exceed in vice. Adam Clarke adds that men suffer not only by injustice but through envy also, so that the encouragement to act an upright part is very little. John Gill fills in the kinds of work meant, the study of arts and languages, the writing of books, or excellence in the mechanic arts, and John Wesley that he meets with envy instead of honour; Charles Ellicott would render the phrase skilful rather than right work.

The folded hands and the handful with quietness raise a question of voice. Keil and Delitzsch report that some read the fifth verse as the objection of the industrious and the sixth as the reply of the slothful, and that one interpreter lapses into a hypothesis of dialogue he rejects elsewhere; they hold that the unity of thought is preserved, and that the rest commended is not the rest of sloth but rest against the activity that robs a man of himself, the hunting after gain that never has enough. Gill takes the other side, reporting interpreters one of whom supplies the word saying at the fifth verse, so that the sixth becomes the sluggard’s apology. Clarke allows both, that the words may be the slothful man vindicating his idleness, content to gain little and enjoy his handful in quiet, or the writer’s own reflection; Wesley takes only the first.

Ellicott weighs the folded hands separately. Interpreters have usually taken the eating of one’s own flesh as a figure for suicidal conduct, but it has been proposed to read it literally as eating his meat, the sluggard doing better who eats in quiet; Ellicott answers that there is no exact parallel to the phrase, and that if this were meant it would have been introduced formally, as by saying the writer praised the sluggard. Keeping the older interpretation, he makes the conduct recommended a golden mean between ruinous sloth and vexatious toil. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same self-destruction, the hands laid in the bosom instead of used, so that the man feeds on his own flesh and wastes away.

The solitary man who works without end draws the moralists. Henry describes a man who would if he could be placed alone in the earth and thinks one mouth enough in a house; he makes himself a mere slave to his business though he has neither child nor brother, and dares not marry for fear of the expense of a family. Clarke draws the same figure, a man at the centre of his own existence and yet as intent on getting money as if he had the largest family, refusing himself the comforts of life out of his own gains. Gill reports a rabbi who took the missing second for a friend, a servant or a wife, preferring the wife, since friendship costs, a servant would be chargeable and a wife more expensive still. Keil and Delitzsch prefer to read the particle as nevertheless rather than also, since the endless labour already includes a restless striving after more. Ellicott adds the one personal note here, that the vanity of toil is especially apparent in a solitary man, that this may have been the writer’s own case, and that the friendship verses following are more cheerful than the rest of the book.
9:
From the man with no second beside him the book turns to the advantages of company, and the voices divide over what company is meant. John Gill takes the occasion to be the solitariness of the covetous man just described, and holds that it is best to take a wife or at least to have a friend to converse with, since man is a sociable creature and it was the judgment of God that it was not good for him to be alone. Adam Clarke is blunter, that married life is infinitely to be preferred to the other, for the very reasons alleged below, which he says require no explanation. Keil and Delitzsch read the same verses the other way: the marriage relation is not excluded but remains in the background, and the author has two friends in his eye who lie under one covering on a cold night and cherish one another, a proof of friendship which they note is treated as such in a rabbinic tract as well. John Wesley keeps it general, two who live together in any kind of society and so support and encourage and strengthen each other. Matthew Henry takes it furthest, first observing that a man who labours to maintain those he loves has more satisfaction than the miser in his toil, then applying the union to Christians, who assist each other by encouragement or friendly reproof and warm each other’s hearts in converse; where two are closely joined in holy love, he says, Christ comes to them by his Spirit, and there is the third strand of the cord.

The three illustrations are then worked over in detail. On the fall, Gill keeps to plain accidents, a man thrown from his horse or out of his carriage or into a ditch and lifted up by his companion. Charles Ellicott notes that the word for woe used here occurs only once besides in the book though it is common in later Hebrew, and adds on the next verse that nights in that country were often very cold and that it seems to have been common to sleep with no covering but the ordinary day garment. Keil and Delitzsch report that one version has confused the word for woe with another, and observe that the verb about raising the fallen man is potential rather than certain, it being possible and probable that the thing will be done provided the companion is a true friend, for which they quote a rabbinic saying.

On the last of the three they weigh the verb. If it means simply to overpower, the sense would be that one can overpower a solitary man while two can maintain their ground against him, as one interpreter takes it; but Keil and Delitzsch object that the conditional particles of the preceding verses will not allow so purely logical a reading, and they see no reason why the word should not carry a sudden assault as well as a completed subjugation, since in later and cognate usage it means to seize or lay hold of. Gill takes the attacker first as a thief or robber whom two together can resist, and then turns the verse to spiritual use: the enemy chooses a believer when alone, as he tempted the first woman in the garden and the Lord in the wilderness, and fellow Christians who know of the temptation can help their friend by advice and by striving together in prayer for him.
13:
The poor wise youth against the old foolish king is the chapter’s hardest passage, and Charles Ellicott says so: the section presents great difficulties, the context gives little help because a new subject is introduced so abruptly, and no confidence can be placed in attempts to find a historical reference. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase about the king who will no longer be warned as a tolerative passive, a refusal to let oneself be enlightened; earlier he was in some measure open to instruction, but in his old age he is hardened in folly, defies all warning counsel and undermines his own throne. Matthew Henry allows the writer to speak freely here because he was himself a king: nothing is more slippery than the highest post of honour without wisdom and the people’s love, and refusing admonition is not a part of a king’s honour but his greatest dishonour, since folly and wilfulness go together and those who most need admonition can worst bear it. John Gill draws the two portraits, the old king venerable for gravity but of small capacity and vicious with it, and the youth not yet come to manhood, poor, his parents unable to buy books or masters.

Two voices look for the story behind it. Adam Clarke reports an old paraphrase that finds it all in the patriarch, a poor child of three years who refused the idols the old foolish king had set up, was cast into a furnace and delivered, and afterwards left that country to reign elsewhere while his persecutor grew poor. Gill instances the young man sold into Egypt, whom a rabbinic source names here, and the youngest son taken from the sheepfold; though one scholar, he adds, reads the line of the old king himself, coming out of a degenerate house to rule. Ellicott finds the Hebrew as ambiguous as the English over whether the poverty belongs to the old king or the new. Clarke, dissatisfied with the ancient guesses, offers a reconstruction of his own: a king abused his power, grew jealous of a son the people were looking to, and shut him up in prison; when the old king was gone the son was enthroned and the multitudes flocked to him; but with the reins in his hands and flatterers about him he too was corrupted.

On the second youth Ellicott parts from everyone. Most modern interpreters, he reports, identify him with the young man of the earlier verse and read that he stood at the head of all his people, yet was popular only for a time and gave the next generation no pleasure; Ellicott answers that by no stretch of rhetoric can all the living who walk under the sun be the subjects of one sovereign. He thinks the writer reverts to his general topic and looked at all the living with the generation that will succeed them: one hardened in its ways and incapable of being admonished, displaced by a new one with which the generation after will be just as dissatisfied. Keil and Delitzsch keep the succession of kings, the words placing the author back at the change of government. Clarke observes that history affords many instances of mean persons raised to power and of kings reduced to a morsel of bread, quotes two Latin lines on fortune making a consul of a rhetorician and back again, and adds from a Roman writer that most people adore the rising sun, though when the new king grows old few regard him and he may be despised by those who welcomed him. Gill calls this an itch of novelty passing from generation to generation, and John Wesley counts three generations in the verse, the authors of the change, their parents and their children, all of one inclination, so that they will weary of a wise successor as their parents wearied of his foolish predecessor.
